utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the sake of the record, could we have the appearances please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. Peter McCloskey, Stefan Waespi, and Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Michael Karnavas for Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, could you please tell us why Mr. Stojanovic was not here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stojanovic is struggling still in the field trying to find witnesses and finalise that part of our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Blagojevic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Mr. Jokic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED JOKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Well, this is a Pre-Defence Conference according to the Rule 73 ter. The purpose of this conference is to help the Defence to prepare their case. Before we start, I believe that we need some clarification from the Defence counsel for Mr. Blagojevic. By the scheduling order of 19th March, 2004, the Trial Chamber ordered the Defence to file its amended witness list by the 5th of April. But up to now, we haven't received any documents at this moment. So could I ask Mr. Karnavas to give us some explanations for that. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I deeply apologise for missing the deadline. It was due to being out in the field and some mishaps. But nonetheless, I do have for today the amended witness summaries, Your Honour, as well as the initial list of exhibits. And I'm prepared to -- I have courtesy copies. I have yet to file it because there was no one at the Registry to file it when I arrived. But I have it ready for the members of the Trial Chamber. And I did communicate with Mr. McCloskey yesterday, informing him that I was running a little late, that I would have it today. I did serve him with a courtesy copy this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please somehow brief us on the contents of that filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For instance, how many witnesses are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. We are proposing a total amount of -- at this moment, at this moment, because I intend to -- or I anticipate, I should say -- at this moment, we have 76 witnesses, Your Honour. I didn't take an accounting as to how many we are proposing through 92 bis. I believe it's somewhere in the neighbourhood of around 30 or so. And I should add that at the moment we have half of those 92 bis witnesses -- statements. We're taking them right now. Ms. Tomanovic is in the field taking the remainder of them so that we could have them by next week. And I'm told that the procedure would be that -- for everyone to look at it. Perhaps we have an agreement as to which of the witnesses would be accepted and then arrangements would be made thereafter to go back in the field to have the statements certified. So that's where we are. We do anticipate having at least at this moment two witnesses where we're going to be asking for the assistance of the Court as a pro forma. We may ask two or three others as well because of their positions. They are in the military or were in the military. One is a general. We're also trying to find and locate a Mr. Tomo Kovac. He did provide the Prosecution with a statement. He has been dodging us for several months, either in Serbia, Montenegro, or various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have made a request from the Prosecution to provide us with their last known whereabouts of this gentleman so we could at least try to locate him. We did -- one witness in particular seems to be pretty obstinate about coming here and that is Mr. Vasic. I did meet with him for three hours. I met with him a second time. He had indicated that under no circumstances he wanted to come here and that he anticipated an illness. And I just received yesterday, I guess an anticipatory letter stating that he is too ill to travel to The Hague, though last time I saw him he was as strong as a bull and in fact, invited me to sit down and drink with him a litre of rakija. So hardly what I would call someone I would call bedridden and unable to travel to The Hague. And I might add he has given approximately six statements to the Prosecution. On one occasion he travelled on his own to The Hague. He is an important witness, an important witness because he's mentioned in the Butler report, an important witness because there are documents that the Prosecution has referred to and has placed a certain emphasis on, and he is also important because of certain information that he as provided the Prosecutor, including a conversation that he had with Mr. Kovac, and also some information that he learned about another individual who is on our witness list, who at the time was a -- the head of the intelligence organ of the Main Staff. And -- so anyway, that's the update. Again, I want to apologise for missing the deadline, but it is rather difficult to meet with witnesses, take statements, and then summarise them in the field, especially when the means are not as adequate as we would like them. I should also add that one of the mishaps was a holiday. We hit one of the weekends and all of our witnesses cancelled as a result of three-day Sava, St. Lazarus. So that was unanticipated. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we'll come to the details of the future witnesses at a later stage. And at this moment, I have to remind you, if you need some help or assistance from this Trial Chamber, please inform us as early as possible. So that might take some time to go through all the procedures. By that stage we could only base on the filings by the Defence on the March 16th, 2004, that is the 65 ter filings, as well as the informal proposals concerning of the 92 bis statement. I understand that the Defence has the intention to call as a Rule 92 bis witness, and this Trial Chamber has received a preliminary list of those witnesses via e-mail. Let me discuss those witnesses. If their names are mentioned, I hope, first I hope we could use the 65 ter numbers. If, just in case, we have to mention the name of the witnesses, we hope the Defence counsel will remind us to go into the private session, just out of the consideration of the precaution. And in this e-mail, we found there are several witnesses proposed by the Defence for the Rule 92 bis witnesses, that is witness number 7, 8, 16, 17, 21, 22, 23, 24, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, and 36. I believe that it's a very preliminary list, and at this stage I would like to ask the Defence counsel to confirm this in this pre-Defence conference to see whether there's some additional witnesses in this list or after second thought they would like to delete somebody from this list. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps it might be best if I could provide you and Judge Argibay with a courtesy copy of the amended list, which would have the -- which has all of the additional witnesses, including the additional 92 bis. I don't intend to delete. We did add to the list, and frankly -- though I would prefer to have each and every one of these witnesses here to give live testimony, I recognise the Court's preference to have 92 bis statements in lieu of viva voce testimony under certain circumstances. But the statements that we will be providing, Your Honours, are going to be very factual and very brief. They are not going to be 20- or 30-page statements. So it's not going to be taxing or burdensome to the record. That's the best I can say at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you: When do you plan to file your request for that admission of the 92 bis statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first, as I indicated, Ms. Tomanovic is in the field finalising these statements. I would suspect that when she returns we will have all those statements, and at that point in time I would be filing that request and thereby you would have not just the names but also the statements that accompany the names. And of course that way the Prosecution would also have the opportunity to make a reasoned judgement as to whether they're going to not oppose, oppose, or maybe even welcome the witness appearing viva voce. So hopefully next week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I think at this moment I have to remind you that under Rule 92 bis E, 14 days notice should be given to the Prosecution, who may object within seven days. Time is then needed to send a presiding officer and obtain the certified statement. In sum, an approximate period one month will be needed between the motion and admission of the Rule 92 bis statement. And at this moment, I couldn't know whether some of them need to be cross-examined by the Prosecution. So I would like to say that it is very important that the motion be filed as soon as possible. Well, let's come to the 65 ter filings of those witness lists, which the Defence proposes that the Courts would hear them live. Frankly speaking, Mr. Karnavas, we believe that some witnesses seem to testify under similar topics. It does not appear from the summaries that each of these witnesses would provide additional information. Could the Defence explain why several witnesses are to testify on the same topic. For instance, could I draw your attention to the witness number 1 and number 2. We could only base on the summaries you kindly provided to us. We found that the only difference are the names, but the contents are exactly the same. So my question is: Do we need to hear those two witnesses, both? I hope that in this courtroom one plus one is equal to two, rather than one plus one is equal to one. We believe that -- judging from the summaries you provided for us, we believe that they are exactly the same. Could you give us some explanations about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Well, the explanation may seem on the face the same. They are two distinct positions these gentlemen hold in that particular community. They happen to be, aside from Mr. Deronjic, the two most important civilian authority members of the Bratunac community. They did play separate and distinct roles during the 12th through the 13th, 14th of July, 1995. Witness number 1 will testify with respect to his meeting with General Mladic, which was held at a different time, albeit basically the same conversation, with witness number 2. He will talk about being ordered to provide humanitarian assistance and the assistance that he did provide. He will be able to give us a flavour as to what the conditions were. He will also talk about his competencies and the competencies of the civil government at the time, because I believe that one of the contingents is whose prisoners they are, who gave authorisation to whomever to send the Muslim males to -- into Bratunac, what were their responsibilities. Also the first individual was present during that rather famous meeting with Colonel Beara on July 13th. The second individual again holds a highly important position in the local government. And again, I must stress to the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution has argued repeatedly that in this joint criminal enterprise, a concept which I don't necessarily agree with, but nonetheless they have argued that the civilian government, or members of the civilian government - which would include the MUP - worked in tangent and sometimes were subordinated to the military. So that's why I think it's essential to have both of these individuals. Both of them have been questioned by the Prosecution, and so we believe that they are both necessary in order to understand the situation in Potocari as it existed during those days. They will also testify, separate and distinctly, that at no given time did they ever see Mr. Blagojevic at any meeting; that at no time was he ever consulted with respect to anything that was going on at the time, including providing assistance for the securing of the Muslim prisoners that were in Bratunac the night of the 12th and the 13th. In fact, they will both testify that based on their observation at the time, that Mr. Blagojevic played no role; in essence, he was a nonentity for all intents and purposes in those days when you had members of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff going about their business, doing whatever they wanted, and using the Bratunac Brigade headquarters as their own forward command post. They will also be able to describe, in my opinion, their own personal observations of Mr. Blagojevic as an individual, as a commander, someone that they had observed, keeping in mind that the Bratunac Brigade had seen approximately ten or more commanders over the past three years. And by all accounts - and I could bring in more than a hundred people at a flick of a finger that will come in here and testify that Mr. Blagojevic was an outstanding individual, professional, and that at no time did he ever cause any problems, and they are absolutely stunned to know that he is here facing these sort of charges, given that at no time he was ever witnessed at anything that would -- could remotely be considered improper. So I think, given their position, given what they were involved with, given that they participated in the humanitarian assistance at the time, given the efforts that were made, both of these individuals are necessary. They also tie in with witness number 3, because this individual is responsible for the mobilisation process, a concept that is rather foreign to someone like myself coming from a country where the government would not -- does not have laws in the books where drills are required and where folks on the ground are trained to instinctively respond to mobilisation calls by the government. That is essential because the Prosecution again, as it has argued and has argued through Mr. Butler, that the speed with which the buses and trucks were able to respond to the scene in order for the evacuation process to take place, denotes that a plan existed well in advance of the attack of Srebrenica. And in fact Mr. -- the third witness will be able to testify that he relied heavily on the assistance of the local authorities, and given his mandate he was able to mobilise not just individuals but also private property as well as state property. So all of these tie in as well as if you go down the list to the civilian protection individuals. What we are endeavouring to do, Your Honour, is to paint a picture that will enable the Trial Chamber to fully understand the -- how this particular place, Bratunac, was organised, how it was able to respond under the circumstances, how you have different civilian organs that are performing certain tasks that may, on their face, appear to be military but in fact are civilian. And so we're trying to do the best we can to give all of the information available to the Trial Chamber, because after all - and this is something that whoever came up with these truncated version of trying cases here, which I dare say are your brethren, and I say this with the utmost respect - nonetheless we have to keep in mind that this is a process that should be open and transparent to the public. And I think that the public deserves to see what exactly happened in and around Bratunac on those days. And again, I want to stress and I will continue to stress throughout this trial, the Prosecution has made it their mission, their goal, to make sure that Mr. Blagojevic dies in prison. That's his stated goal. He's indicated that he wants a life sentence for this man. So when I take -- when I use the test of proportionality, I don't have to go too far. So I don't think that we're going to benefit by saving a day or two or reading a few less pages. So that's -- and again, I want to stress that I've narrowed this list quite a bit. And again, I'm willing to negotiate, if necessary. And there is a third option, a middle way, which would be depositions. I'm always willing to, you know, go down that ally with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, frankly speaking, I believe that this summary of the 65 ter filings is poorly drafted, because what you said was not reflected in this summary. We could only work on the basis of your filings. And of course if the testimony of a witness goes to the acts and conducts of the accused, it could not go through the 92 bis procedures. But anyway, I believe that the witness summary should indicate why in the specified additional information that each additional witness that each witness would provide because we try to avoid as much as possible the repetition of the testimony of the witnesses. So if you are not considering to have one of these witnesses go through the 92 bis procedure, I hope you could consider trying to reduce the time you used in the direct examination, especially on those parts which is apparently repetitive. As for the witnesses that testified concerning the evacuation out of Potocari, we have several witnesses on this topic. We also could not be helped from your summaries. So I would like to ask you: Are you going to consider more 92 bis witnesses on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I could be -- I could give it some additional thought, Your Honour, if the Court wished for me to look at some particular witnesses. However -- and again, the reason I kept the summaries short because when I write too long, there are complaints that I'm going beyond the page limitation. So I try to keep it as succinct as possible. And perhaps in doing so, some of the meanings was lost. Again, with respect to the evacuation, the Prosecution has repeatedly argued, especially through Mr. Butler, that the Bratunac Brigade played a significant role in the evacuation in various ways. One, you had Mr. Butler saying that there were numerous soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade in Potocari on the day -- on 12th July, 1995. There -- certain commanders and soldiers were seen on the video footage, so there's no denying that they were present. Of course, mere presence alone is not sufficient to amount to criminal activity, though an inference could be drawn, and I suspect that the Prosecution will argue, that their presence in and of itself demonstrated a threat or a force. And therefore, a conclusion can be drawn that they were there for purposes of intimidation. Recognising that that is a potential argument that will be made by the Prosecution, and one that I would make if I were in their shows, though I am not, I believe it is imperative that I bring as many of these witnesses here so they can explain in detail and so that you can judge their demeanor, and perhaps even pose questions to them, as to why on earth they were in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995. So that's why. Now, we have a great deal. If you look at my new list, which has significantly increased, you will see several new members of the Bratunac Brigade military police. And again, I'm willing to pare them down. I'm willing to do the 92 bis if necessary. But of course I begin with wanting the most and perhaps willing to settle for the absolute necessary. But I again would like the Court to look at this amended list with the summaries, because again they, each and every one of them, reflect their observations as to why they were in Potocari. Some went there because they were curious. Some went there because they were ordered by Mr. Nikolic, at least this is what they will testify. And again, I think it's necessary to have them here so we can look at them and we can ask them questions or the Prosecution can cross-examine them with great gusto, if they wish, as to what they were going, what they observed, who ordered them, and what have you. Some are absolutely necessary, because at least one of them, as we note, was actually ordered and was under the belief that he was seconded to Colonel Jankovic. And that is significant, that is a significant factor because later on we will learn that it is Colonel Jankovic, at least to this individual's belief, that does the orders of the male Muslims to -- into Potocari -- I mean, into Bratunac on the afternoon of 12 July. So I understand the Court's predicament, but I would say that at least for the first couple weeks my list is relatively harmless. I can be as efficient as possible. I don't -- my timing that I put down are rather on the generous side, I must admit, on the generous side. And I'm willing to do a very tight direct examination. But I certainly want to bring as many people as possible here because I think Mr. Blagojevic deserves to have members of that community, his soldiers, coming in, his commanders who were there, to give an explanation. And I also think that the Court will have an invaluable lesson when they hear from these people and they will come to the conclusion that Mr. Blagojevic was a well-respected commander who never ordered any of his men to do anything. So that's where we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. We found the same problem with the witnesses 11 and 12. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The numbers have changed Your Honour, so if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the 65 ter filings, number 11 and 12, you could read the summaries. They are almost the same, almost the same, and as well as the number 13 and 14; those two are almost the same. We could not get some assistance from your filings on that, so the same questions are in our mind. Do we need, as you said, as many witnesses to testify on the same issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to be argumentative or disputatious, though some may say that that's my nature. But given that you have these concerns - and I must confess that in drafting the first list I was trying to be rather concise and perhaps I was less than explicit, so if the Court could look at this new amended list and direct me to provide further clarification in writing as to any particular witness, I can do so. In the meantime we can proceed as scheduled with the first couple witnesses, three witnesses. So I don't believe that the court proceedings would not be held up and nobody would necessarily be prejudiced, unless Mr. McCloskey has a particular comment or objection as to the first three or so witnesses. I believe if I were to -- if I were given some guidance as to which ones you had problems with, I could certainly sit down and elaborate in greater detail and not take your valuable time here in giving lengthy explanations. And I apologise for not being as thorough as I should have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a good suggestion. When we received your latest filing, we believe that it's necessary to hold another meeting between the parties or whether it's a 65 ter or not. We'll concentrate on the witness list and we'll try to help you to concentrate on certain points. For your information, I would like to remind you, as I said before, that we believe that witnesses 1 to 10 are somehow repetitive. They testified on the same meeting, the same matters. And as for witnesses 27, 28, 34, 37, they will testify about the role of the military police and Mr. Nikolic's involvement. As for the witnesses 25 and 26, they all will testify about the locations by military police. And there was some securities provided to Mr. Mladic. The witnesses numbered 29, 30, 32. And this is our concern at this moment, because we could only work on the submissions provided by you there. We don't have any other more information on it. So this is our preliminary concern. I hope this matter could be solved during the next meeting, based on the new filings submitted by you today or yesterday. Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Another matter is about the details provided in the witness list. We have already mentioned that a little bit, but in the filings of March 22nd, 2004, the Prosecution requested additional information with respect to a number of witnesses. These witnesses are number 3, 4, 6 to 8, 13, 14, 16, 17, 24, 25, 31 to 33, and 35 to 37. I believe that the Defence has already received that filing, so we could hear the response from the Defence on this very matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did receive the filing, and rather than respond, because I was on my way to the field, what I did was went back and in my amended witness summaries I incorporated some further information that would assist the Prosecution, hopefully, in its preparation for cross-examination. I should note that, I think with the exception of one of two of those witnesses, those witnesses identified by the Prosecution were listed as 92 bis witnesses. And therefore, I believe that upon receiving the statement itself, the Prosecution should at least be satisfied as to the nature of what exactly the witness is going to be testifying to, so they're not going to be prejudiced by that. But they'll have the statement itself. And as I indicated, I anticipate having those statements filed by some time next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I mentioned before, that you are going to file that 92 bis filings with the statement. And for those witnesses you proposed to go into the 92 bis procedures, I believe the Prosecution will have an opportunity to go over those statements and to make the proper response on that issue. But there is still some witnesses which are live witnesses. I would like you to concentrate on those witnesses, especially the witnesses 3, 4, 6, 13, and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I've indicated, Your Honour, that in my -- in this pleading that I'm about to file today - I was actually finished 7.00 this morning, so I didn't have a chance to file it - I further elaborated as to what those witnesses would be testifying to. I am hopeful that the clarifications and the amplifications would satisfy the Prosecution's concerns. I did provide them with a courtesy copy. I am sure that they have not had an opportunity to digest my thoughts. And again, as I've indicated during our 65 ter meeting, that I'm always willing to sit down with the Prosecution and provide them with any additional information. So I believe that's my response to your concerns, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Karnavas, the problem is that the summary of the witness statements lacks the specificity, especially concerning the witnesses 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, and 20. We have a big problem with your 65 filings -- let alone the Prosecution. Maybe I could hear the Prosecution on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, the Prosecution had significant problems identifying much in the way of any detail on lots of this, as we stated in our motion. In fact, we were -- tried to be very conservative in that motion. In areas where we had witness statements, such as the first two witnesses on the list that you've already spoken of, we didn't put them in our motion because we do have witness statements from them and so we can at least glean something from our own witness statements. That, of course, I don't believe is something the Court has the benefit of, so that obviously puts the Court in a difficult situation. But as I hear Mr. Karnavas's description of those first two witnesses, much of what he mentioned was not in any of these witness statements that we have. These were witness statements that were from 1998, were relatively brief, and the specific references to his client were very -- were not mentioned by the witnesses in the statements. So even the ones we didn't mention on our motion are of some concern, though I look forward to reading Mr. Karnavas's brief. I hope there's more -- I'm sure there's more information that I hope will reflect the testimony of the witnesses. Because, yes, this is an important obligation on the Defence. It's a new obligation in the practice of law, but it is an important obligation. And so I had similar difficulties and look forward to reading his brief and would hope we would get more informations even on witnesses 1 and 2, as aside from the -- just the brief verbal recitation we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to respond to that just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has been working on this case since 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These witnesses have been available to them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me give you some guidance. Do you have additional statements of those two witnesses, beyond the scope of the statements they made to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If they haven't asked the question, they're not going to get the answer. If they fail to ask the necessary questions because they weren't interested in the answers, it's not my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that. I'm saying that is your fault. I'm just saying that -- do you have the additional statements of those two witnesses, because we're going to hear them very soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stated what they're going to testify about. The Prosecution took extensive statements from them, extensive statements from them. And they're not precluded from meeting with these individuals if they want to go back and question them again. You know, it's pretty simple, what they saw, what they did. So you know if the Trial Chamber wishes for me to write a three- to five- or ten-page statement as to what each and every witness is going to say, I can do that. That's not a problem. I can provide that in that sort of detail. So that's not a problem. A summary, in my estimation, is a summary, a summary to what they're going to testify to. If I say "character," then that should be enough to alert the Prosecution that they're going to testify about Mr. Blagojevic's character. We're not dealing with alibi. I'm not putting on any witnesses who are going to say that he's in We're not going to say he's in Banja Luka, when he's in fact in and around Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you still did not answer my question. We don't want you to furnish with the Chamber and with the party, the other party, a ten-page statement at this stage. But your summary should be up to the point to indicate what is the additional information you're providing through the direct examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I still fail to see the Court's concerns. As I indicated there are statements of these two individuals. The direct by and large is going to be based on the statements that they gave and the information that they gave, and perhaps some logical questions that should be been follow-up, should the questioner at the time wanted that additional information but for whatever reason chose not to obtain it. So I believe I have answered Your Honour's questions. There's an addition to what I've stated on the record with respect to witness number 1 and witness number 2, there's nothing more for me to add. If the Court wishes for me to reduce that in writing, I can do that. But with respect to witness number 3, I did the same thing. But let me point out for the Trial Chamber, for instance, one concern that the Prosecutor had. It had to do with one witness who testified at the sentencing hearing of Mr. Nikolic. Now, I find that absurd that they're asking me to clarify something that they already know. And they want to know what the motive is of the -- when it's crystal clear and I pointed it out in great detail and one need only go back to the record. So do I need to write an essay on what this individual is going to say? We also have to consider the resources that are allocated to the Defence. I don't have five or six or ten assistants to be out there in the field while at the same time I'm supposed to be here. But I'm willing to comply with the rules as they're stated. Now, if there are any concerns with respect to any particular witness, I'm willing to amplify. But I believe that the summaries in and of themselves are mostly sufficient, and again if pointed to the right direction, I can certainly amplify the Trial Chamber with more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. As this stage, the Trial Chamber invites the parties to sit together and solve this problem about the insufficient information. If problems still remain, the Trial Chamber remains available to provide some assistance. The parties are invited to contact the legal officer in case of problems. Let's come to the next issue, and should we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session. And I have some questions to ask the Jokic Defence team, and that is I wonder if you have any interest in some of the witnesses that are announced to testify in the Blagojevic defence, which means that do you want to direct examine some of the witnesses, especially concerning the burial or reburial operations. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would probably have to respond in general terms. Of course, if there are some burial and reburial operations mentioned by the witnesses brought here by Mr. Blagojevic's Defence team, we would be interested in cross-examining these witnesses. But quite frankly, I haven't seen the list of the witnesses composed by Mr. Blagojevic's team yet. And probably if it's filed, it's sent to Mr. Stojanovic's locker and I don't have the key of that locker; I have a completely separate locker. And I'm not receiving those mails from the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I inform you about the number of those witnesses which you might look into it and give us an answer sometime at a later stage. That is number 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, it's about the role of the civilian protections concerning the burial, reburial, as well as the witnesses 6, 7, 8. I understand that they will testify on the burial operation at Kravica warehouse on the 14th and the 15th of July, which may be relevant to the Jokic Defence. We say "might," which is not definitely relevant. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I have told you, I haven't seen the list of the witnesses, Your Honour, so I really don't know the contents of the testimony and I don't know the names. And probably, as you mentioned, we will have to have another either 65 ter conference or Status Conference before the trial, that probably would take place next week by the time Mr. Karnavas can file additional motions that at that time will be able to answer these questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the next issue is about the expert witnesses. In the filing of 22nd March, 2004, the Prosecution has asked the experts that are to be called, as witnesses should be intimated to them and the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber understands that the Defence does not intend to call any expert witnesses. Could I have the confirmation from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know where the Trial Chamber got that idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the 65 ter filings. There are no expert witnesses listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that was the initial list, Your Honour. On the amended list, we did provide -- we have the name of one expert. In fact, she is coming to The Hague and we'll be having access to certain documents via the Prosecution -- that are in the Prosecution's hands. And we anticipate that she will be completing a report well in advance, perhaps five or six -- five or seven weeks, maybe even earlier than that, before she is to testify. In the new filing, I also make reference to some witnesses such as Mr. Trivic, who testified before. And given -- in light of his position and his knowledge, we will be asking questions that are directly related to his field of expertise. So he could, in essence, be, I guess, considered an expert, though he was a Prosecution witness. And again, he would be testifying as to what's already before the Court, nothing new. So that's what I foresee. There may be one other witness -- expert witness. At the moment, we are reserving our options. That decision will be made very shortly. I understand the time limitations, but it's something that needs to be given a little more thought in spite of several months of preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. We only hope that we could get that expert witness's statement as soon as possible, because it will take some time for us to make any decisions on that. The next issue is about protective measures. In the Defence case, we will proceed as we did during the Prosecution's case, which means that the party calling the witness has the responsibility to inform the Trial Chamber about any protective measures concerning the individual witness who is going to testify here in the courtroom. Generally speaking, as for the usual protective measures, we will grant the requests. However, it should be reminded that the requests for the closed session should be made in advance and also need the proper grounds. In the similar way, requests for subpoenas should preferably be filed about a month in advance in order to be effective. The next issue is about exhibits. The Prosecution has requested that the Defence states whether it intends to use any other exhibits, apart from those that the Prosecution has provided previously. I don't know whether in your latest filing, Mr. Karnavas, you have a list of the documents. Could I hear from you for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have something to be filed today. It does have some additional documents. I -- what I -- what we have done is itemised what we believe at this moment the documents are going to be -- that are already in the record. And we itemised them as Prosecution exhibit, Defence exhibits, and whether they're ours or Mr. Jokic's, and then we have a section on additional. We anticipate that that list might grow somewhat, but I don't anticipate it to -- for that list to grow in any great detail or -- you know, it's not going to be anything that would prejudice the Prosecution. As soon as we identify something that we believe we are going to be using as an exhibit, we will alert the Prosecution well in advance. But at the moment, I don't foresee a whole lot. We have provided the translation department with certain documents to be translated. Mainly there are the rules on maps from the VRS. There are some rules that relate to witness number 3 with respect to his functions. So basically that's what we're looking at. But by and large, we took advantage of the generous disclosure material provided to us, and we were able to put into evidence as much as we wanted during the Prosecution case, and the Prosecution of course was -- relied on a great deal of its own evidence, which we will probably be making reference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any problem with the translation issue at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We put it on a fast track. They are extremely helpful. We don't tend to wait until the last moment. And we were told that we would have it -- we would have this material well in advance, so hopefully we'll have it soon. We also, I believe, submitted some statements as well, the 92 bis statements that were already obtained. And I believe they were given for translation as well. So that -- as it comes in, we try to be on top of everything, keeping in mind that it is rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think there are some organisational matters I would like to mention at this stage. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, the rule that we the Prosecution was going by was that two days before the witness testified we would give the Defence a list of the exhibits. I just wondered if that rule is in effect, and if I could also get Mr. Karnavas's assurance that he would provide us with this B/C/S rules for the third witness. That person will be here before we know it, and rules need a study. And so if we could get those rules as soon as possible, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think there's any problem on this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's no problem. The only -- there's no problem. I can check with the translation. Frankly, I can't put my hand on it. I mean, there's a technical problem, one that I am sure that Mr. McCloskey understands, should something happen to Ms. Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I hope you have the priority list there and make -- those documents need to be translated in an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They were already issued for translation, Your Honour. But I will see if I can dig something up today and provide it to them. Not a problem. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as for the organisational matters of the trial, the statements of the witnesses, if there are any, should be transmitted to the Chamber in advance. The list of the witnesses for a week to come as well as exhibits used through each witness should be known beforehand, whatever two days, at least two days, or a week in advance. In urgent situations, you could send it by fax or e-mail, like you did, Mr. Karnavas, to the Chamber and the OTP just to let us be prepared. At this stage, I would like to know whether the Prosecution agrees with the lists for the first week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean the list of the witnesses the Defence is going to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection to anything we see. We're just -- some more information on a few of them would -- that's all I would ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any problems of logistics regarding the witnesses to be called in the first week, Mr. Karnavas? For instance, the visa issues, the transportation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. We -- part of the -- part of our function in the field was also to assist them with getting their passports; that's another issue because some of them don't have that. And so -- but we don't believe that's going to be a problem. We've been in communication with the folks who make those arrangements, and so we believe that they're going to be here at least the day before they testify and the first person testifies. And that would be enough time for me to meet with the witness. So I don't anticipate that, and hopefully -- I would suspect that the first couple weeks are going to be a little rough. But once we get into a rhythm, we'll be able to move along quite quickly. And I think as the Court will see that -- we won't be wasting too much time on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And from that list, we didn't see any exhibits attached to those witnesses. Could I know whether you are going to use any exhibits. Or if so, would you please be kind enough to provide us as well as the other party that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Court wish for me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't aware. I thought that was just a declarative statement. Well, Mr. President, I don't anticipate having to use any exhibit lists with the first two witnesses -- any exhibits. Basically it will be just a narration of what they saw and what they did. I suspect that the Prosecution may wish to use their statements, but barring that I don't anticipate having the need for these two witnesses. Though, I will give it some more thought. With respect to the third witness, there is -- there are some exhibits, though I'm not -- frankly, I'm prepared at this particular moment to identify them. And in light of the logistics of trying to get everything ready, perhaps within the next -- within a short period of time we'll be able to identify it well in advance the particular exhibits we intend to use with each witness. And of course to provide the Prosecution with advance notice, at least two days in advance, as to any particular exhibits, though I don't think we are going to be copying them, as they did for us, because I don't believe that we'll be able to handle that. But we'll see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for the estimated duration of the opening statement for Mr. Blagojevic's Defence, and I understand that you indicated that you need three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's going to take the full day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Three hours is quite a long time, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I could -- see there again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are not going to testify in this Tribunal. We hope we could have more time to hear the witnesses, rather than to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Because I know that opening statement is not evidence, but I guess I was trying to be cogent when I wrote my summaries. And so I thought I would take some liberties in providing a thorough analysis of the case. Even if -- it probably will take less than three hours, Your Honour. I will try to do it perhaps as little as one session; however, because of the logistics, as we were told by the folks that make the arrangements for the witnesses, we will not be able to have a witness for that first day. So it doesn't mean that I intend to take the entire day simply because I have it, but I just want to make sure that the Court understands that we did try to make arrangements for the witnesses to be here much earlier in anticipation of having one. But we were told that because of the holiday and because of some of the other logistics on that end, they preferred bringing the witness at the latest possible date. And so that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there's two things I would like to remind you. That is, preparing your opening statement. I hope you could take into consideration of the 98 bis decision made by this Trial Chamber. The second issue is that -- well, if you couldn't -- if we could not hear the witness on that day, it does not mean that you have the whole day. Don't you think it's necessary for us to have some time for the preparation to hear the witness the next day? So if we don't have the witness, we'll stop and leave much more time for each party to be prepared for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And I will take into consideration the 98 bis decision. Though I must say I was somewhat disappointed in some areas and I was hoping to address them in the opening. But I agree. Just because I have three and a half hours doesn't mean I should try and take all three and a half hours. I will try to do it in one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The last issue is the length of the trial. The Defence indicated that before the end of the Prosecution's case as well as at the 65 ter meeting that it would need 10 to 12 weeks to present it case. Do you, Mr. Karnavas, confirm this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I confirm that that's what I noted back then. As far as confirming that that's what I anticipate in the future, I would have to disappoint the Trial Chamber. I believe it might take a little bit longer. And, you know, again I know the Trial Chamber wishes for us to move expeditiously, and there's always that tension between, you know, finding the right balance. We'll try to move as fast as possible. There may be some -- in light of the Court's concerns, there might be a possibility of reducing the viva voce list of witnesses. But I forecast, I forecast, that it will probably take us until the end of July. Now, I don't intend to drag it on anymore than I have to, Your Honour. But I want to have as much leeway as I can to put on the best possible case I can for Mr. Blagojevic, you know. And so -- but I will take your concerns to heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think on the average and in the -- on the average and in the practice of this Tribunal, the Defence case takes less time than the Prosecution's case. That's the usual practice. Because you don't have to prove your client is innocent, even after the decisions of the 98 bis. And you don't have to present a kind of an overall situation, the background situation, like the Prosecution did. The evidence you presented should be only directed against the Prosecution's evidence presented in their case. And as you know, in your case the much -- the Trial Chamber has much leeway for the leading questions, because some of the issues we have already heard and are familiar with in the Prosecution's case. And at the same time, as you said, the parties could have another meeting concerning of the 92 bis witnesses. I appreciate your effort that you promise to do your best to streamline your case, but try to do your best to make greater effort in this aspect. So the Trial Chamber will give you about 11 weeks to present your case. Try to do your best. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, how long do you think you need to present your case? I think in the 65 ter meeting you indicated that you need six weeks to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what I heard from Mr. Stojanovic, that he anticipates six weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, for the same reason that we believe six weeks are just too long, could you please consider ten weeks -- would you consider the four weeks -- I'm sorry about that. The four weeks to finish your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll do our best and I'll transfer your message to my lead counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope so. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage are there any other issues that the parties would like to mention this to Bench? Yes, Mr. Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just one issue that may help the Prosecution prepare its eventual case, and that is the issue of whether the -- either of the accused are going to testify and how they may choose to speak. That's something that I think is normally announced at some point during the proceedings, and we of course would be benefited by -- the sooner announcement on those matters, the better. Also, regarding the military expert, and I appreciate Mr. Karnavas has said that he will give us a decision soon on that, if we could have some kind of a deadline so we -- because this is a rather significant potential witness, a military expert. They've taken many times days to testify in the past. So if we could have a little more than soon so we had an idea of at least a deadline to work with on this point. Because it's really well beyond the time to announce for the military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, there are two questions posed to you by the Prosecution. One is about the expert witness. The other is about the statement or testimony by your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, I don't believe -- I'll deal with them in order. With respect to whether a client is going to testify or give a statement, it's my firm conviction that that decision gets to be made whenever and if ever by the client at any stage of the Defence case and that no limitations or impositions should be made on the defendant. Because he or she can wait and see how the Defence case progresses and may decide for whatever tactical reasons to give or not to give a statement, to testify or not to testify. And I don't think under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that an accused is required to give notification at this point in time. I certainly think that it is good practice for -- before the Defence resting its case, for the Trial Chamber to inquire whether the accused wishes to give a statement or whether he waives or whether he wishes to testify or if he does not whether he does so on a freely and voluntary basis. So lest there be any claims later on of not knowing his or her rights or being coerced into not testifying or testifying. So that's my position on that first issue. On the second issue, I agree with Mr. McCloskey that a deadline, you know, would probably be in order. And I'm hoping to have an answer within the next couple of weeks. In part, I understand that it does take some time to prepare for military testimony, military expert testimony. But again, again testimony from a military expert would be to rebut the testimony already provided by Mr. Butler. And -- so it's not -- we're not dealing with rocket science. It's just something that's already, I'm sure, very handy in Mr. McCloskey's memory and he's able to recite, in fact probably, Mr. Butler's various reports. But I would hope to have a decision within two weeks. Again, in light of the Court's limitations on timing, I have to streamline. So I'm trying to use the best I can and also resource-wise. So to the extent I can use other witnesses that are qualified, other individuals who are mentioned and are capable of elucidating the rules and the procedures of the VRS, then of course it wouldn't -- I could achieve my goal without bringing somebody and spending one or two weeks on a military expert. So that's why I'm hedging my bets at this point in time, not that I'm trying to sandbag Mr. McCloskey. And I think he knows me -- that's not my practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have to remind you that we have to move fast, because the time at our disposal is not sufficient I must say. Well, at this stage, Mr. Karnavas, do you have anything to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think I've -- I think that your pointed questions have exhausted me at this point in time and I think we've covered pretty much all of the issues that needed to be covered. Again, I wanted to extend my apologies for missing the deadline. I will have this amended witness summary in today. I will file it right after the hearing today. I dare say after the questions posed to me, it might not meet quite the specifications, but I would like to get it in and then again I will meet with Mr. McCloskey after he's had a chance to review it and see if we have some way of streamlining this -- the witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind that this is a Status Conference, if I understood correctly at the beginning of this session, I would like to point certain things out, although I'm really fed up by now. But I do have to say it. About certain measures in order to prevent my position from deteriorating completely. I don't believe a word that the person from my imposed Defence has said. And I am really concerned about my safety, security, and the circumstances that are resulting from all this. You must believe me when I say that this kind of conduct from my Defence, which I refuse to recognise and accept from the moment when I was forced to deny my confidence to that person because his acts and his behaviour at the time, which means a year ago, even before this trial started, caused me great concern and astounded me. To this day, I am responding before two indictments practically, one indictment raised by the Prosecutor, brought by the Prosecutor, and the second indictment involving charges of bribery and corruption by this second person. It has to be decided finally who is guilty, he or I, because nothing has been done so far concerning that second indictment. This is a great and real concern for me. I see no way out. I will try to do everything I can. And I also want to touch upon the question raised by the Prosecutor, whether I would be testifying or not. I think the Rules are clear. I have the right to testify, but how? Under what circumstances? In which way? I could say a lot under oath, because an oath is a thing to be believed. Truth stands behind an oath, and I know the truth. The person from the Defence team that was foisted on me is trying to handle this in a way unparalleled in legal practice anywhere, and I believe it has no justification, can have no justification. And I beg you to find a way to think of some measure to deal with it. You said that you would inform the Appeals Chamber of my requests and demands. I am crying out for information. I am completely -- I am completely without any information. I am sitting in prison, where I'm supposed to die. What does it mean to die? Is that what the Prosecutor wants, for me to die? Based on what am I supposed to live or die? Some facts are being presented here, and based on those facts other facts are levelled. And the Trial Chamber is supposed to decide, rather than individuals who are making their own calculations and documents and papers that they have. I am astounded, and all of this is really affecting my very survival in these circumstances because of the situation that has resulted from what I've just described. I beg you to make sure that everything decision that is made is in the interest of law and justice, rather than be made formally for the sake of procedure and completion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just merely address this one issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there's a need to do that, if you are going to say something about the accused's fate in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The only issue -- and I will leave it to the Court to address, because I know you know the answer, the accused may think there is something been said about this to counsel, and of course there is absolutely nothing been said to counsel. This is Mr. Karnavas -- we know he's just over-arguing the situation. So -- And I'm sure I don't need to say anything more to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Karnavas, as I explained to you many times before, that we have a decision made by the Appeals Chamber. I understand that you are not quite satisfied with the findings of the Appeals Chamber at this moment, but as a rule and as the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, we have to comply with the decisions made by the Appeals Chamber. And last time you mentioned that you believe there are some mistakes in that decision. The issue is that you have to point them out in a specific way, in which specific paragraphs, in which areas those mistakes occurred. If you claim that the whole decision is wrong, I'm afraid there is a very little chance to review that decision. But if you say that there are certain areas, certain allegations, or certain facts are not correct, I'm not quite sure at this moment, but I think, myself, there is a chance for the review concerning of those areas. My advice is: Discuss it with Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas is a very good counsel in dealing with those issues. Try your best to seek the advice from Mr. Karnavas. From his professional training, it is my belief that Mr. Karnavas will point out the areas for you and discuss it with you on those areas. And then you will decide whether to file a petition or not to the Appeals Chamber on certain areas. As for your statement and testimony, it all depends on your free will. You have to understand, it is a rule in this Tribunal that you are still innocent until proven guilty, as well as you cannot incriminalise yourself by your own testimony. If you choose to make a statement or give the testimony under oath, you have - I must stress that - you have to consult this matter with your counsel to seek his advice on this very issue. Because sometimes you may not understand the implications of your testimony or your statement on the merits. Yes, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for situation number one regarding the public and revised decision of the Appeals Chamber, I cannot judge -- I am not in a position to judge why the Appeals Chamber made such a public and revised decision with the contents that it has. It lacks -- it does not contain the key issues which led the Registrar to make a wrong decision regarding, first of all, that lawyer who is now working in the field. I wonder who she is doing there. And furthermore, to make another wrong decision which was accepted again by the Appeals Chamber. And then the Registry failed to conduct the basic investigation to ascertain whether that is right or not. That is why I am asking the question: Who is guilty of bribery and corruption in this court? He or I? And why in this situation -- how can you advise me to cooperate with him? That is absolutely impossible. It is out of the question. He accused my family; he accused me. He made me into a thief, a criminal, and he continues to represent me. That's absolute nonsense; it's absurd. It has nothing to do with Defence counsel in the sense that I understand and accept. That's on issue number one. On issue number two regarding my testimony, I have no fear of self-incrimination. I have no dilemma whatsoever in this respect. I will say what I have to say, and that is the only thing that I can say. I will say what I know. I have no fears and I don't need the advice of a lawyer who doesn't wish me good. That advice would be superfluous. I will say all that I know with regard to the relevant time, my role, my position, what I did, where I was, all my communications, and all the rest. I can state all that the best way I know how as I understand it. I can recount all the events and how it came about, that I became the commander of the Bratunac Brigade at the relevant time. I have no concern about that whatsoever, and I expect from you to give me a chance to present all these facts, because that could perhaps dispel all the doubts and suspicions that we can hear being voiced here as to whether this or that person is lying or not. I am entitled also to present certain facts regarding myself, and whether I'm guilty or innocent is something that is up to you to judge after hearing my testimony under oath. Because of all the things that are being orchestrated here and the resulting circumstances, I kindly ask you not to limit any further my rights which have deteriorated considerably as it is. I wish to exercise the rights given me by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the statute, because it is my historic role and duty to present you with my view, with my statement. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I'll be very brief, since we have been sitting here for almost two hours. As for the first issue, I could not agree with you, Mr. Blagojevic. There is no indictments against you, as you said. One is about the indictment issued by the Prosecution, and the other is about some other matters. We do not think thus the indictment at all. And I would like to draw your attention to the decisions made by this Trial Chamber that we will designate a legal representative to help you to communicate with your counsel on certain issues. I believe that you have received the B/C/S versions of that decision made by the Trial Chamber, and I'm very disappointed that you did not take advantage of this mechanism. But I can assure you that this opportunity still exists -- is still available for you to use it. I hope you could make the best use of it. The second -- as for the second issue -- well, on the one hand, I think this Trial Chamber will according to the rules; and on the other, we have to guarantee that your right is not affected by your own testimony. It is a very complicated legal issue. On this very issue, I hope you could have several discussions with your lawyer. I believe he is very professional in this field. This is all I could say at this stage. So having said that, I believe that the hearing is adjourned.
